action_criteria.label: Order MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast (tumor protocol with DWI, FLAIR, post-contrast T1) to characterize the right frontotemporal lesion, define mass effect, and plan surgery
action_criteria.rationale: Contrast MRI with diffusion characterizes the ring-enhancing lesion, separates the features of tumour and abscess as far as imaging can, defines the mass effect that governs lumbar puncture safety, and plans the approach (EANO 2021).

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform a lumbar puncture with 4 mm midline shift and ventricular compression: the pressure gradient risks herniation.
Do not initiate tumor-directed therapy (radiotherapy or temozolomide) before tissue diagnosis is established.
Do not start therapeutic anticoagulation without a clear thromboembolic indication, given the upcoming neurosurgical procedure and bleeding risk.
Do not use enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs (phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital), which lower dexamethasone and temozolomide exposure.
required_recommendations: Refer urgently to neurosurgery for stereotactic aspiration and biopsy of the right frontotemporal lesion with frozen section, Gram stain and culture, proceeding to maximal safe resection once tumour is confirmed; send the specimen for an integrated histomolecular diagnosis (WHO CNS5).

Start dexamethasone for symptomatic vasogenic edema (for example 4 mg every 6 to 8 hours after a loading dose when mass effect is marked) at the lowest effective dose, with glucose monitoring and gastric protection, and taper after surgery.

Start antiseizure treatment with levetiracetam for the documented focal seizures with impaired awareness and left arm clonic activity (at home and during the examination); this is treatment of tumour-related epilepsy, not prophylaxis. Avoid enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs (phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital), which lower dexamethasone and chemotherapy exposure.
Monitor capillary blood glucose closely on dexamethasone in this patient with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.8%), and add insulin as needed.
Hold aspirin before the neurosurgical procedure; it is taken for primary prevention only.

Withhold empirical antibiotics until the aspirate is obtained while he remains clinically stable and the procedure can be done within about 24 hours (ESCMID 2024), so that Gram stain and culture are interpretable; if antibiotics become necessary, choose a regimen compatible with the penicillin allergy (rash).

After the integrated diagnosis, refer to the neuro-oncology multidisciplinary team; at age 48 with KPS 80, the standard for glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype is radiotherapy 60 Gy in 30 fractions with concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide (Stupp 2005; EANO 2021), noting that the unmethylated MGMT promoter predicts less benefit from temozolomide.

patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. Kowalski is a 48-year-old right-handed high school history teacher who presents to the emergency department after experiencing his first witnessed seizure at home this morning. His wife reports that while eating breakfast, he suddenly stopped talking, stared vacantly for several seconds, and then his left arm began shaking rhythmically. The episode lasted approximately 30 seconds and was followed by confusion lasting about 5 minutes. He has no recollection of the event.

For the past three weeks, he has experienced progressive headaches that are predominantly right-sided, worse in the morning upon waking, and partially responsive to ibuprofen. Over the past week, the headaches have become more severe and are now accompanied by nausea, particularly when bending over or straining. His wife has noticed that he has become increasingly forgetful and has been slower to follow conversations, which she initially attributed to stress at work. Two days ago, he had an episode at school where he lost his train of thought mid-lecture and stood silently at the podium for about 10 seconds before resuming, which concerned his students enough that the school called his wife.

Of particular concern is that six weeks ago he underwent extraction of a lower right molar complicated by a dental abscess. Because of his penicillin allergy he was treated with a 10-day course of clindamycin. His dentist cleared him at a follow-up visit two weeks later, noting the socket was healing appropriately. A non-contrast CT head obtained in the emergency department showed a right frontotemporal hypodense lesion with surrounding edema and 4 mm leftward midline shift.

He also reports a single episode of optic neuritis at age 31. He was evaluated for multiple sclerosis at the time with brain MRI that showed two small non-specific white matter lesions. He was followed by neurology for two years without further events and was ultimately not diagnosed with MS. His sister was subsequently diagnosed with relapsing-remitting MS six years ago.

He denies any recent fevers, chills, night sweats, or weight loss. He has not traveled recently and has no exposure to tuberculosis. He denies any history of cancer, though his father died of lung cancer and his paternal uncle died of a brain tumor.
